MUQATIL:17:29-30/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:17:29-30/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:17:29-30/r1.claim: The command teaches proper spending: do not hold back from spending on what is due out of miserliness.

MUQATIL:17:29-30/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:17:29-30/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:17:29-30/r2.claim: Do not give away everything, leaving yourself unable to give when asked.

MUQATIL:17:29-30/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:17:29-30/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:17:29-30/r3.claim: People will blame the person who gives nothing; maḥsūr means left cut off or stranded.

MUQATIL:17:29-30/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:17:29-30/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:17:29-30/r4.claim: He links maḥsūr with 67:4, glossing ḥasīr as one left exhausted or cut off.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p131/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p131/r1.speaker: الحسن
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p131/r1.claim: Al-Hasan says not to withhold spending on God's due, nor spend outside it; either extreme leaves one blamed and unable to help others.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p131/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p131/r2.speaker: قتادة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p131/r2.claim: Qatāda says not to withhold one's hand from obedience and God's due or spend it in disobedience and waste.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p131/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p131/r3.speaker: السدي
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p131/r3.claim: Al-Suddī takes the image as a lesson about spending: neither keep one's hand closed nor spend until nothing remains; the result is blame and loss.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p377#2/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p377#2/r2.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p377#2/r2.claim: Qatada reads the hand bound to the neck as withholding from spending, and stretching it fully as wasteful extravagance.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p377#2/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p377#2/r3.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p377#2/r3.claim: A spendthrift ends blameworthy among God's servants and remorseful over what he squandered.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p254/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p254/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p254/r1.claim: Maḥsūran describes a gift that exhausts and leaves you stranded, like travel that wears down a camel; the root means to exhaust.

TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r1.claim: The tied hand is a simile for withholding obligatory spending; the open hand warns against giving away everything and having nothing when asked.

TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r2.claim: The needy blame a person who cannot give, while the spender blames himself for quickly exhausting his wealth; محسورا means depleted and disgraced.

TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r3.claim: The root حسير describes an animal worn out by travel, a gaze exhausted at its farthest reach, or anything spent and weakened; the verse also uses this word for exhausted sight.

TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r4.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r4.claim: Al-Hasan says not to withhold from spending or to squander.

TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says the verse concerns spending: do not withhold good or spend wastefully, then blame yourself after losing all your wealth.

TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r6.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v14p573#2/r6.claim: Another saying from al-Hasan warns against stinting God’s provision or spending in disobedience, lest He remove what one has.

TAB-FULL:v14p576/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p576/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v14p576/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the tied hand as miserliness.

TAB-FULL:v14p576/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p576/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v14p576/r2.claim: Qatada says not to withhold from God’s obedience and right, or spend in disobedience and wastefully; the result is blame among people and regret for what passed.

TAB-FULL:v14p576/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p576/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v14p576/r3.claim: Another Qatada report paraphrases the warning as neither withholding nor squandering, leaving the person blamed and remorseful.

TAB-FULL:v14p576/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p576/r4.speaker: ابن جريج
TAB-FULL:v14p576/r4.claim: Ibn Jurayj says to spend the required rights, avoid prohibited spending, and expect blame as a sinner and exhaustion from having nothing left.

TAB-FULL:v14p576/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p576/r5.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v14p576/r5.claim: Ibn Zayd says not to refuse every good gift, then spend on lawful and unlawful things until nothing remains for a later requester, who may blame you for whom you aided.

ZAJJAJ:v3p236/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p236/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p236/r1.claim: The bound hand and the hand spread fully mean neither be miserly nor spend extravagantly.

ZAJJAJ:v3p236/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p236/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p236/r2.claim: فتقعد is subjunctive as the consequence of the prohibition; محسورا describes someone exhausted by overburdening himself.

NAHHAS:v2p422/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p422/r3.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p422/r3.claim: Hand is feminine; neck may be masculine or feminine, but masculine is more common, as the cited anonymous verse shows; its damma is dropped for heaviness.

NAHHAS:v2p422/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p422/r5.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v2p422/r5.claim: He explains maḥsūr as exhausted, like an animal worn out by being driven too far.

NAHHAS:v2p422/r6.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p422/r6.speaker: قول آخر
NAHHAS:v2p422/r6.claim: Another explanation is that regret has overtaken the person.

SULAMI:v1p386#3/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p386#3/r1.speaker: أبو سعيد القرشي
SULAMI:v1p386#3/r1.claim: The Prophet was directed away from both extravagant giving and withholding, toward balance in every condition.

SULAMI:v1p386#3/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p386#3/r2.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p386#3/r2.claim: Do not withhold what is not yours or claim credit for giving: God is the true owner and people are only distributors of their due; a prophetic report says God gives and the Prophet distributes.

THALABI:v6p95#3/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p95#3/r10.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
THALABI:v6p95#3/r10.claim: Jabir recounts that a boy asked for a shirt for his mother; the Prophet gave away his only shirt, remained naked, and missed prayer, prompting the verse about avoiding total depletion.

THALABI:v6p95#3/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p95#3/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p95#3/r7.claim: A hand tied to the neck means withholding money due in rightful spending; do not be miserly.

THALABI:v6p95#3/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p95#3/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p95#3/r8.claim: Do not give away everything, leaving yourself blamed by those asking and depleted with nothing left to spend.

THALABI:v6p95#3/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v6p95#3/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v6p95#3/r9.claim: محسورا means left exhausted and empty; the root also describes a spent animal and a weary eye, and Qatada adds regret over past spending.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p287/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p287/r1.speaker: عبد الله
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p287/r1.claim: ʿAbd Allāh reports that a boy asked the Prophet for a shirt for his mother; he gave away the only one he had and sat bare, prompting the warning against either hoarding or exhausting one’s means.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p287/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p287/r2.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p287/r2.claim: Jābir b. ʿAbd Allāh gives a similar account: a child asked for his mother’s clothing, the Prophet gave his own shirt, and companions later found him unable to come out for prayer.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r1.speaker: المنهال بن عمرو
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r1.claim: A woman sent her son to ask the Prophet for clothing; when she asked for his shirt, he gave it to him, and the verse was revealed.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r2.claim: The root ghalla means insertion or putting inside; Imru al-Qays uses it for an eyelash inserted into the eyelid.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r3.claim: To embezzle from spoils is called ghalla because the stolen item is hidden in a sleeve; a hand in shackles is likewise described as inserted into iron.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r4.speaker: ابن عباس والمفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r4.claim: They take a hand shackled to the neck as an image of stinginess and withholding God's due in alms and family ties.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r5.claim: The command means do not keep the hand completely closed against giving good.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r6.speaker: صاحب النظم
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p316/r6.claim: He says Arabic favors describing the hand as habitually shackled rather than saying it was shackled in a single act; the verse forbids a settled habit of withholding, not restraint when restraint is appropriate.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r1.claim: He takes the prohibition on opening the hand all the way as a warning against giving away all one's spending and gifts.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r2.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r2.claim: They take it as a prohibition on wasteful spending, spending in disobedience, and spending on what is improper.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r3.claim: The phrase has two interpretations: do not spend everything even in obedience, or do not squander money as Mujahid and Qatada explain.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r4.speaker: السدي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r4.claim: He says the person ends up blaming himself and being blamed by others.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r5.claim: He glosses mahsūr as having nothing left.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r6.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r6.claim: He glosses mahsūr as being left cut off and without support.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r7.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r7.claim: Arabic calls a camel mahsūr when its journey is exhausted and its progress stops; the verb describes driving an animal until it can no longer continue.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r8.speaker: ابن قتيبة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r8.claim: He says giving can exhaust and cut off the giver just as travel exhausts a camel; the root also means to use up everything someone has, as with an exhausted animal or eye.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r9.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p318/r9.claim: He interprets mahsūr as regretful for what one has done, though the author notes that the usual active forms for regret are ḥasir or ḥasrān, not mahsūr.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:17:28-29/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:17:28-29/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:17:28-29/r3.claim: Do not hold back all charity as if your hand were tied to your neck, nor spend everything in gifts.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:17:28-29/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:17:28-29/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:17:28-29/r4.claim: The verse was revealed when the Prophet gave away his shirt and then had nothing to wear to go out, so he remained at home.

JISHUMI:v6p4194#2/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4194#2/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4194#2/r2.claim: Ḥasr is uncovering; ḥasrah is grief over what has slipped away, and a spent animal is exhausted; maḥsūr is depleted after losing what one had.

JISHUMI:v6p4194#2/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4194#2/r7.speaker: جابر
JISHUMI:v6p4194#2/r7.claim: A child asked the Prophet for a garment for his mother; having only his own shirt, he gave it to her, remained naked when the call to prayer came, and the verse was revealed.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r1.speaker: جابر
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r1.claim: Jābir's childhood request for a coat led the Prophet to give away his only shirt and miss the prayer; the verse was revealed in this setting.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r2.claim: The bound hand means withholding rightful expenditure; the opposite warning is against giving away everything one owns.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r3.claim: Requesters blame someone who withholds; maḥsūr describes the exhausted person left with nothing to spend.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r4.claim: Maḥsūr describes someone exhausted and without money, or a spent animal; its root also describes persistent questioning.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r5.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p90/r5.claim: He glosses maḥsūr as regretful about what one has done.

TABRISI:17:29/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:17:29/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:17:29/r1.claim: A hand tied to the neck portrays refusing to give; spreading it fully portrays giving away everything and becoming wasteful.

TABRISI:17:29/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:17:29/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:17:29/r2.claim: The image of a fully spread hand is a metaphor for extravagance; ‘blamed’ means one blames oneself and others blame one.

TABRISI:17:29/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:17:29/r3.speaker: السدي
TABRISI:17:29/r3.claim: ‘Exhausted’ means left with nothing and no means.

TABRISI:17:29/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:17:29/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:17:29/r4.claim: ‘Exhausted’ means left with nothing and no means.

TABRISI:17:29/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:17:29/r5.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:17:29/r5.claim: Alternatively, it means incapable and regretful.

TABRISI:17:29/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:17:29/r6.speaker: أبو عبد الله ع
TABRISI:17:29/r6.claim: Alternatively, it means stripped of clothing and naked.

TABRISI:17:29/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:17:29/r7.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:17:29/r7.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī explains the outcomes together: if stingy, one sits blamed; if extravagant, one remains distressed and regretful.

TABRISI:17:29/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:17:29/r8.speaker: الكلبي
TABRISI:17:29/r8.claim: Al-Kalbī says that giving everything leaves nothing for later requesters, who then blame the giver.

TABRISI:17:29/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:17:29/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:17:29/r9.claim: A report says a woman sent her son to ask the Prophet for a garment; when told to ask for his shirt, he gave it, leaving himself unable to dress for prayer and prompting unbelievers to mock his absence.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r1.claim: Ibn Masud reports that a boy asked the Prophet for a shirt on his mother's behalf; the Prophet gave his own shirt and remained bare, after which the verse was revealed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r2.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r2.claim: Jabir's version adds that the call to prayer came, the Prophet did not emerge, and companions entered to find him naked; the verse was revealed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r3.claim: The verse forbids both complete withholding and spending or giving everything, which leaves the giver blamed and exhausted.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r4.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r4.claim: Ibn Qutayba says maḥsūr is exhausted by the gift, like a camel worn out by travel and left behind.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r5.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r5.claim: Al-Zajjaj says maḥsūr is someone who has reached the utmost fatigue and exhaustion.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r6.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p29#2/r6.claim: Abu Ya'la says the warning is aimed at people who may regret what they give, not the Prophet, who saved nothing, or the confident Companions who gave all they owned.

RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r1.claim: After commanding expenditure, God teaches its proper measure; the believer’s balanced spending in 25:67 is the model.

RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r10.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r10.claim: Spending the amount needed for the month leaves a person helpless midway through it, bringing blame from family and dependents for poor planning.

RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r2.claim: A hand bound to the neck pictures withholding so severely that one neglects oneself, family, kinship, and good works.

RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r3.claim: Spreading the hand fully means spending excessively until nothing remains.

RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r4.claim: Ethical teaching treats every trait as having blameworthy extremes; miserliness is excessive restraint and wasteful spending is excessive outlay.

RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r5.claim: The virtuous character is the just middle course, linked to the description of the community as balanced.

RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r6.claim: The one who is left blamed reproaches himself, while companions blame him for wasting all the money and exposing dependents to hardship.

RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r7.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r7.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says a camel is called exhausted when its travel is cut short; the verb describes driving an animal until it can no longer continue.

RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r8.claim: The plural ḥusrā follows the pattern of words such as قتلى and صرعى; the verse about the returning gaze uses ḥasīr for exhaustion.

RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r9.speaker: القفال
RAZI-FULL:v20p156/r9.claim: Al-Qaffāl compares the person who spends everything to a traveler whose mount fails: needed money carries someone through the month or year as a camel carries a traveler to the next stop.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r1.claim: These instructions concern charitable spending; spending on corruption is forbidden whether little or much.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r2.claim: The verse discourages exhausting one's resources in response to the first needy person, lest later people or one's dependents be left without support; a maxim says every extravagance has a neglected right, and the ruling depends on each person's circumstances.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r3.speaker: ابن عرفة
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r3.claim: Ibn ʿArafa says one who squanders wealth ends up exhausted and unable to spend or act, like a spent camel; 67:4 uses ḥasīr for a tired, depleted gaze.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r4.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r4.claim: Qatāda interprets maḥsūran as regretting what one has spent; al-Qurṭubī objects that the active form for regret is ḥasir or ḥasrān, not maḥsūr.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29#2/r5.claim: A person is malūm if blamed for wasting wealth or if denied assistance by someone who reproaches him.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r1.claim: A hand shackled to the neck is a metaphor for the miser whose will cannot release anything from his wealth, like a shackle restraining the hand.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r2.claim: In Bukhārī and Muslim, Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet's parable of miser and giver in iron cloaks: charity loosens the giver's clothing while the miser's rings tighten; Abū Hurayra saw the Prophet gesture to show it.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r3.claim: Stretching the hand fully pictures losing one's wealth: a closed fist retains what it holds, while an open hand lets it go.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r4.claim: Although addressed to the Prophet, the verse means his community, since scripture often uses their leader as their representative in Arab usage.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r5.claim: The Prophet saved nothing for the next day and endured hunger, while some Companions spent all their wealth; he did not condemn them because of their certainty and insight.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r6.claim: The prohibition targets excessive spending by someone who fears regret over what he gave away; one who trusts God's promise and reward is outside the intended warning.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r7.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r7.claim: Another view makes the address specific to the Prophet, teaching him moderation in spending.

QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r8.speaker: جابر
QURTUBI-FULL:17:29/r8.claim: Jābir and Ibn Masʿūd relate that a boy requested a shirt for his mother, so the Prophet gave his own and remained at home without clothes until people entered and found him naked; the passage says the verse was revealed then.

BAYDAWI-FULL:17:28-30/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:17:28-30/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:17:28-30/r4.claim: The bound hand and fully outstretched hand are figures for stinginess and waste; the command is for generous moderation.

BAYDAWI-FULL:17:28-30/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:17:28-30/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:17:28-30/r5.claim: Excessive spending leaves one blamed by God and people for waste and bad management, exhausted and empty-handed or regretful.

BAYDAWI-FULL:17:28-30/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:17:28-30/r6.speaker: جابر
BAYDAWI-FULL:17:28-30/r6.claim: Jabir reports that a child asked the Prophet for a shirt for his mother; the Prophet gave him the shirt he wore and remained without one at prayer, and this verse was revealed.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p285/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p285/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p285/r1.claim: Bound hand and hand spread fully illustrate miserliness and extravagance; kull is an accusative verbal noun, and the command is moderation between the two.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p285/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p285/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p285/r2.claim: The squanderer is blameworthy before God, people, and himself when later need brings regret; maḥsūr means depleted and unable to go on, or bareheaded.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p285/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p285/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p285/r3.claim: A Muslim woman wagered with her Jewish co-wife that Muhammad was more generous than Moses; her daughter asked for his shirt, he gave it and sat naked, missing prayer, whereupon the verse was revealed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r1.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r1.claim: One occasion report says the verse came after the Prophet gave away his only shirt and was left naked.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r10.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r10.claim: Blame corresponds to miserliness and exhaustion to spending everything; the two outcomes describe the two extremes of the conditional warning.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r11.claim: The verse consoles the Prophet: limited means do not signal God's contempt or stinginess, since provision expands or contracts by divine will and wisdom for servants' benefit.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r2.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r2.claim: Another report says the Prophet gave one hundred camels each to al-Aqraʿ and ʿUyayna, then raised al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās's fifty to one hundred before the verse came.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r3.claim: The verse uses concrete images for abstract conduct: miserliness is a hand bound to the neck, preventing it from moving to give.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r4.claim: The hand represents giving and receiving; spreading it represents spending money away, while closing it retains what is held.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r5.claim: The paired images balance one another: a bound hand is a forceful closing and an open hand disperses its contents; Abū Tammām also used this contrast.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reads the verse as a representation of the miser and the squanderer and a command to the middle course between extravagance and stinginess.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r7.claim: The apparent addressee is the Prophet's community: the Prophet kept nothing for the next day, and Abū Bakr could give all his wealth through complete trust in God.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r8.speaker: ابن جريج وغيره
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r8.claim: Ibn Jurayj and others explain the command as not withholding required charity and not spending on what God has forbidden.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r9.speaker: قالون
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v7p41#2/r9.claim: Qālūn is reported to read al-basṭ with ṣād.

SAMIN-DURR:17:29/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:17:29/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:17:29/r1.claim: كل البسط is an accusative cognate object, annexed to its مصدر.

SAMIN-DURR:17:29/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:17:29/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:17:29/r2.claim: فتقعد is subjunctive as the result of the prohibition.

SAMIN-DURR:17:29/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:17:29/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:17:29/r3.claim: ملوما can be circumstantial or a predicate.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r1.claim: A divine hadith reported by Abu Hurayra says God commands the Prophet to spend and promises to spend upon him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r2.claim: Two angels pray each morning that a spender receive compensation and a miser suffer loss.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r3.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra says charity does not diminish wealth, pardon increases honor, and humility before God brings elevation.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r4.claim: A report from Abdullah ibn Amr warns that greed destroyed earlier peoples by leading them to stinginess, severing kinship, and immorality.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r5.claim: A report from Burayda's father says giving charity frees a person from the jaws of seventy devils.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70#2/r6.claim: A report from Ibn Masud says one who spends economically will not become poor.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r1.claim: The verse commands moderation, condemns stinginess, and forbids wasteful spending.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r2.claim: A hand tied to the neck means miserly refusal to give; this resembles the Jews' charge that God's hand is tied, though God is generous, as stated in 5:64.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r3.claim: Extending the hand fully means spending beyond one's means or income.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r4.claim: The verse uses folded pairing: stinginess leaves one blamed and shunned, as in Zuhayr's poem; overspending leaves one depleted like an exhausted animal, and hasir describes an eye tired from looking in 67:3–4.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd, and others explain the verse as prohibiting both stinginess and extravagance.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r6.claim: A report in both Sahih collections compares a miser and a spender to men in iron coats: generosity loosens and lengthens the coat over the body, while stinginess makes its rings constrict.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r7.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p70/r7.claim: The Prophet tells Asma to give freely and warns that hoarding or counting tightly will cause God to withhold from her.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p375/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p375/r10.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p375/r10.claim: The hand imagery condemns both miserly restraint and unbounded giving: either exceeds balance, bringing blame or leaving one depleted.

DURR-FULL:v5p271/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p271/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p271/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says a hand tied to the neck means giving nothing, while opening it fully means giving away everything; the latter leaves the giver blamed and exhausted by those already given to.

DURR-FULL:v5p271/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p271/r7.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v5p271/r7.claim: Ibn Umar says spending on oneself and one's family for God's reward earns reward; provide first for dependents, then the nearest relatives, and give any remainder away.

DURR-FULL:v5p273/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p273/r4.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v5p273/r4.claim: Giving away all one's property leaves one with nothing; the hand should neither be restrained nor opened without limit.

DURR-FULL:v5p273/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p273/r6.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v5p273/r6.claim: The Prophet told a wealthy man to pay obligatory alms, maintain kin, and recognize the rights of the asker and poor neighbor; he then cited the command to give kin, needy people, and travelers without waste.

DURR-FULL:v5p275/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r2.speaker: يسار بن الحكم
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r2.claim: When the Prophet generously distributed Iraqi wealth before some Arabs could ask, the balanced-spending verse was revealed, warning against being left blameworthy and empty-handed.

DURR-FULL:v5p275/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r3.speaker: المنهال بن عمرو
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r3.claim: A woman asked the Prophet for clothing through her son; he gave the boy his own shirt, and the verse was revealed.

DURR-FULL:v5p275/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r4.claim: A boy conveyed his mother's request for the Prophet's shirt; the Prophet gave it and sat bare, after which the verse was revealed.

DURR-FULL:v5p275/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r5.speaker: أبو أمامة
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r5.claim: The Prophet repeatedly told Aisha to spend what was at hand; she worried nothing would remain, and the balanced-spending verse was revealed.

DURR-FULL:v5p275/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r6.claim: The image of a hand tied to the neck means miserliness.

DURR-FULL:v5p275/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p275/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas applies the command to spending: do not withhold good or spend wastefully, lest one blame oneself for lost wealth.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r1.claim: Being left depleted means that all one's wealth has gone.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r10.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r10.claim: The Prophet said that one who spends moderately does not become poor.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r11.claim: The Prophet said that a person who is economical never becomes poor.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r12.speaker: عبد الله بن شبيب
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r12.claim: Good planning joined with chastity is better than wealth accompanied by extravagance.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r13.speaker: مطرف
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r13.claim: Mutarrif says the best matters lie in the middle course.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r14.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r14.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r14.claim: A report from the Prophet says management is half of livelihood, kindness half of intelligence, worry half of old age, and few dependents one of two forms of ease.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r2.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r2.claim: Hasan reads the verse as forbidding both extravagance and miserliness.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r3.claim: The person is blamed by other people and depleted of money.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the expression as embarrassed and ashamed, and says Arabs use it that way.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r5.speaker: الشاعر
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r5.claim: An unnamed poet's line is cited as Arabic evidence for the word محسورا.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r6.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r6.claim: The Prophet taught that moderation in one's livelihood is better than commercial wealth.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r7.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r7.claim: A person's practical wisdom includes managing his livelihood well; seeking what sustains him is not love of worldly life.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r8.speaker: أبو الدرداء
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r8.claim: The Prophet said that sound judgment includes gentleness in one's livelihood.

DURR-FULL:v5p277/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r9.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
DURR-FULL:v5p277/r9.claim: The Prophet described economy in practical affairs as half of livelihood.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p136/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p136/r1.speaker: سيار أبو الحكم
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p136/r1.claim: Sayyar reports that after receiving a large grain donation, the Prophet generously distributed it; when people arrived after it was gone, the verse against stinginess and excessive spending was revealed.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p136/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p136/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p136/r2.claim: Ibn Mas'ud reports that a boy asked the Prophet for his shirt on his mother's behalf; he gave it away and sat at home bare, prompting the verse against either hoarding or spending everything.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p136/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p136/r3.speaker: أبو أمامة
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p136/r3.claim: Abu Umama reports that the Prophet told Aisha to spend everything on the back of her hand; she replied that nothing would remain, and the verse followed. The report suggests it was Medinan.

BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r1.speaker: أهل التفسير
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r1.claim: The chained hand and the fully outstretched hand are twin images warning against stinginess and extravagance and urging the middle course of generosity.

BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r2.claim: Do not withhold rightful spending until unable to give, nor give away everything until nothing remains; either extreme leaves a person blamed or destitute.

BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r3.claim: The two prohibitions govern ‘you become’; blame before God and people follows withholding, while regret or depletion follows total spending.

BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r4.claim: The cited Persian poem praises the balanced middle path across all affairs as the best course.

BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r5.speaker: الكواشي
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r5.claim: Al-Kawashi says the address is to the Prophet though intended for others, since he was so open-handed he saved nothing for the next day.

BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r6.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v5p115#2/r6.claim: Al-Kashifi recounts a Muslim-Jewish wager that Muhammad was more generous than Moses, then a mother’s request for his shirt; he gave it to her daughter and missed prayer while left unclothed, prompting the verse.

BURSEVI:v5p116/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p116/r1.speaker: برهان القرآن
BURSEVI:v5p116/r1.claim: A report says prayer time came while the Prophet was embarrassed to emerge unclothed; companions entered, saw him, and blamed him, so ‘blamed and exposed’ is read literally.

BURSEVI:v5p116/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p116/r2.speaker: الإرشاد
BURSEVI:v5p116/r2.claim: Al-Irshad rejects that report because the sura is Meccan while the incident occurred in Medina; the author leaves the matter to God.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r1.claim: The chained hand depicts stinginess and the fully extended hand depicts wasteful spending; both are forbidden in favor of balanced, praiseworthy generosity.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r10.speaker: سيار أبو الحكم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r10.claim: Sayyar Abu al-Hakam reports that after the Prophet distributed a shipment from Iraq, some Arabs arrived to request a share after it was gone, and the verse was revealed.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r2.speaker: ابن عباس عن النبي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r2.claim: A Prophetic report from Ibn Abbas says the person who acts moderately does not become destitute.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r3.speaker: ابن عمر عن النبي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r3.claim: Ibn Umar transmits the Prophetic saying that economy in spending is half of livelihood.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r4.speaker: أنس عن النبي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r4.claim: A report from Anas attributes sayings to the Prophet: planning is half of livelihood, friendliness half of reason, worry half of aging, and few dependents one of two kinds of wealth.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r5.claim: A common saying holds that careful management with chastity is better than wealth joined to extravagance.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r6.claim: The spender becomes blameworthy before God and people; محسورا means regretful and distressed, or exhausted and left with nothing, from the image of a travel-worn person stranded.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r7.speaker: الراغب
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r7.claim: Al-Raghib distinguishes حاسر, who has used up his own strength, from محسور, whom exhaustion has depleted.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r8.speaker: بعض المحققين
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r8.claim: One explanation says the outcome illustrates extravagance's harm at the end, while stinginess is ugly from the outset; some investigators instead distribute the warning across both extremes.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p65/r9.claim: فتقعد is subjunctive as the result of both prohibitions, while blame most directly refers to the image of the chained hand.

ELMALILI:17:23-38/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:17:23-38/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:17:23-38/r1.claim: Elmalılı renders balanced spending through the image of neither tying one's hand to one's neck nor opening it completely, which leaves one regretful and exposed.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p77/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p77/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p77/r8.claim: The warning against waste follows the command to spend by association with its opposite; restraint preserves resources for required giving, and after discussing this aside the passage returns to giving and then explains limits on spending.

TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r10.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r10.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r10.claim: Jaʿfar recounts that the Prophet gave away an ounce of gold, then lacked anything for a petitioner; God taught him that giving all one has leaves one destitute.

TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r7.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r7.claim: Even lawful giving becomes waste when a person gives away all his money and is left with nothing.

TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r8.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r8.claim: Al-Qummi transmits Jaʿfar’s gloss that al-maḥsūr means unclothed; another report in this passage uses it for poverty.

TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r9.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r9.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:17:23-39#3/r9.claim: Ajlan reports Jaʿfar giving dates to successive beggars and recounting how the Prophet gave a woman his shirt; God taught measured spending, and al-iḥṣār is poverty.

TABATABAI:17:23-39#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:17:23-39#4/r1.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:17:23-39#4/r1.claim: Ibn Sinan reports that Jaʿfar demonstrated the two expressions by closing his hand and then opening his palm.

TABATABAI:17:28-30/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:17:28-30/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:17:28-30/r3.claim: The hand chained to the neck is a metaphor for miserly withholding; spreading it fully is spending everything and keeping nothing, so the verse strongly rejects both stinginess and excess.

TABATABAI:17:28-30/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:17:28-30/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:17:28-30/r4.claim: After spending everything, one sits blamed by oneself and others, exhausted and unable to meet ordinary needs, or stripped bare and unable to face or interact with people.

TABATABAI:17:28-30/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:17:28-30/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:17:28-30/r5.claim: Another interpretation makes blame the result of withholding and regret the result of extravagance; the author says this reading and the equation of all spending with waste are not established.

TABATABAI:17:28-30/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:17:28-30/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:17:28-30/r6.claim: Spending all one owns for God or on deserving recipients is not necessarily waste or corruption, so the verse does not imply regret for money that was not misused.

ASAD-NOTES:17:29#n35/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:17:29#n35/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:17:29#n35/r1.claim: The image of the hand shackled to the neck is a metaphor for miserliness, especially unwillingness to help others.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The Qur’an’s detailed natural path matches the Torah’s Ten Commandments: human nature and ancient revelation agree, and rebels among Quraysh or Israel will be punished.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The straight-path details correspond to the prior sūrah’s verse 90, the Torah’s Ten Commandments, and human nature; Abraham, Moses, and Jesus all taught them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Tying the hand to the neck depicts extreme stinginess, while leaving it loose depicts squandering.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: After warning against waste in verses 26–27, the verse prescribes balance: moderate spending on permissible needs and fulfillment of others’ rights, avoiding indigence that leaves them unmet.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:17:29/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:17:29/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:17:29/r1.claim: Both stinginess and wastefulness are excesses and therefore forbidden; generosity is the balanced middle between them.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:17:29/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:17:29/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:17:29/r2.claim: Excess means spending beyond what reason and religion approve, or in unsuitable ways; deficiency means withholding what is due where it is needed.

STUDYQURAN:17:29/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:17:29/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:17:29/r1.claim: The image of a hand shackled to the neck metaphorically condemns miserliness, also criticized in several other Quranic passages.

STUDYQURAN:17:29/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:17:29/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:17:29/r2.claim: A wholly open hand represents irresponsible generosity that can leave one unable to support oneself; the passage teaches moderation between stinginess and waste.

STUDYQURAN:17:29/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:17:29/r3.speaker: Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabarī
STUDYQURAN:17:29/r3.claim: Miserliness brings condemnation from those denied charity; prodigality invites condemnation from oneself, others, and God by quickly depleting one's wealth and leaving one destitute through foolish excess.

STUDYQURAN:17:29/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:17:29/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:17:29/r4.claim: Maḥsūr can mean either destitute or exhausted and depleted.

STUDYQURAN:17:intro/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:17:intro/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:17:intro/r9.claim: Believers are exhorted to virtue and charity, avoid idolatry, murder, adultery, dishonesty, excessive curiosity, and pride, and perform obligatory prayers and night vigil.
